bagley_paper.file: BAGLEY-2026-threat-vectors-cerberus.pdf (local copy supplied by the requester; 25 pages)
bagley_paper.title: Threat Vectors and the State of the Art in Defense Methods for Security in Neurotechnology
bagley_paper.status: arXiv preprint. No journal reference, DOI or venue comment in arXiv metadata; treated as not peer reviewed.
bagley_paper.requester_name_check: The request refers to 'Dr Bryace Allen'. The document prints 'Bryce Allen Bagley' (arXiv: 'Bryce-Allen Bagley'). 'Bryace' is a misspelling of Bryce, 'Allen' is part of the given name, the surname is Bagley, and the document prints no title such as 'Dr'.

cogits.use_in_this_paper: The term appears once, as shorthand for 'specific interpretable intents, thoughts, etc.', attributed to Bagley and Petritsch. The paper argues that most BCI hardware records at a scale where signals cannot be cleanly segmented into individual cogits or into specific physiological operations, so machine learning is needed to decode them, and deep learning models are open to reconstruction attacks. It uses this to argue that reconstruction attacks on neural data are inevitable and that differential privacy should be applied. It does not define cogits formally and proposes no protocol built on them; it says only that 'Bagley and colleagues are working on protocols for cognition' (reference [24], a 2025 workshop talk).
cogits.definition_in_source_paper: Bagley & Petritsch (arXiv:2403.07945v4, Methods 2.1) define cogits as qubit-analogue cognitive state variables, named after 'Cogito ergo sum': a maximally general description able to combine any number and type of cognitive state variables (beliefs, preferences, attitudes) into one vector, analysed with projective ('quantum-like') probability and hyperdimensional computing. The authors stress that this is a statistical formalism and not a claim about quantum physics in the brain. They hypothesise, without empirical test, that the statistics of high-dimensional cogit vectors correspond to the distinguishability of individuals, and they use the formalism to pose the attacker's and defender's algorithmic problems for privacy and autonomy of cognition.
cogits.caution: Cogits are a theoretical construct with no empirical validation reported in either paper.

threat_vectors: 2.1.1 Supply chain: hardware Trojans, firmware replacement or corruption, counterfeit device swapping, key readout with temporary physical access
2.1.2 Harvest now, decrypt later (cryptographic) and an inferential variant (store neural data now, decode with future models)
2.1.3 Air-gap attacks: covert channels, side channels (EM, power, timing), fault injection, high-power electromagnetic pulses
2.1.4 Hardware that fails to isolate software (Spectre, Meltdown, Rowhammer class)
2.1.5 Ransomware, including blocking stimulation or prosthesis control (described as a projected scenario)
Attacks in combination (chains across the above)
2.2.1.1 Brain as attack surface: seizure induction through stimulation, autonomic modulation, interference with motor function or prostheses
2.2.1.2 Substrate alteration: pharmacological or structural changes that raise vulnerability, including accidental cases
2.2.1.3 Neural signals reachable outside the brain parenchyma; unintended pickup by over-sensitive devices
2.2.1.4 Neural identity: fMRI, EEG and sEMG as implicit biometric identifiers; weak anonymisation; longitudinal profiling
2.2.1.5 Cognitive processes: private information inferred from responses to visual prompts; modulation of decision making toward unsafe behaviour; cognition and behaviour as an output channel
2.2.2 Acquisition and modulation devices: implanted, minimally invasive, non-invasive (the last judged most exposed)
2.2.3 Connected devices (phones, computers) with weaker or shorter security support
2.3.1 Interception: analog front end and ADC probing, Bluetooth sniffing, handshake man-in-the-middle, MAC spoofing, passive eavesdropping
2.3.2 Signal injection at the acquisition layer (RF injection, citing Armengol-Urpi et al. 2023)
2.3.3 Spoofing and replay of synthetic or recorded neural signals
2.3.4 Software applications: injection flaws, authentication and session weaknesses, insecure deserialisation, third-party SDK and dependency risk

2.3.5 Cloud: provider breach and session hijack; malicious or vulnerable containers and runtime escape; ingestion API abuse; storage contamination, cross-tenant leakage, noisy-neighbour degradation of real-time loops

2.4.1 Training-time ML attacks: data poisoning, poisoned public datasets, transfer-learning backdoors, adversarial concept drift, federated poisoning, backdoors (adversarial filter, clean label, weight manipulation, compiler level)
2.4.2 Inference-time ML attacks: adversarial perturbations and universal perturbations; Figure 2 also lists backdoor trigger delivery, RF signal injection and analog EM interference
2.4.3 Extraction: model inversion, membership inference, model stealing; Figure 2 adds harvest-now-decrypt-later
2.4.4 ML pipeline attacks: model registry substitution, retraining hijack, monitoring evasion, deployment configuration tampering
defences_recommended: Differential privacy, including differentially private federated learning
Zero trust or deny by default
Neural data stewardship (information-fiduciary duties; permissioned-ledger audit)
Device identity: hardware roots of trust, secure boot, signed firmware, remote attestation
Acquisition-layer hardening: shielding, filtering, runtime EMI detection
BCI-specific defence architectures (described as research prototypes)
statements_of_limits_in_the_paper: The authors say they are not aware of any published demonstration of reconstruction attacks on neural data, and call such attacks inevitable (a projection).
No dedicated fNIRS spoofing attack has been demonstrated.
No well-validated quantitative methods for cognitive anomaly detection exist, to the authors' knowledge.
BCI-specific defence frameworks exist as research prototypes; no ratified defence stack comparable to TLS exists.
The review is described as a snapshot and not perfectly exhaustive.

proposed_values.citation: Tapal P, Bagley B-A. (2026). "Adversarial Vulnerabilities of Neural Biomarker Identification Systems." arXiv:2609.01856v1 [cs.CR] (preprint).
proposed_values.qif_relevance: Second Cerberus-affiliated paper. Black-box spoofing tests of EEG biometric authentication across three recording paradigms. Result is mixed and paradigm dependent; relevant to TARA identity-spoofing entries.

items.verification_method: arXiv API (export.arxiv.org) returned 2609.01856v1; title and authors match. arXiv HTML full text fetched; results section and conclusion read directly.
items.finding: Digital-only test on six public datasets with nearest-centroid, Gaussian naive Bayes and linear SVM authenticators; attacker holds a stolen recording and sees only accept or reject. Adaptive perturbation raised false acceptance on RSVP by +0.032 and +0.051 over baselines of 0.103 and 0.111; motor imagery stayed near zero; on resting-state EEG an unmodified impostor recording was already accepted at 0.812 to 0.896 and perturbation gave negative lift (-0.034 to -0.054), which the authors describe as a paradigm failing without an adversary.

proposed_mapping.note: Spoofing lift is small on RSVP, absent on motor imagery; resting-state weakness is not an attack effect.
Threat model assumes a stolen prior recording.

items.rationale: New 2026 evidence on neural biometric spoofing; direction of the result is easy to misreport, so it is recorded explicitly.

The authors make no claim of code execution from the SDK memory-corruption candidates they list.
items.evidence_level: hardware (link layer) plus dataset-level (ML attacks), preprint

proposed_mapping.note: Unencrypted BLE EEG streams on three named consumer devices.
MITM via MAC spoofing on consumer BCI hardware. Current source (Martinovic 2012) is a side-channel study, not MITM.
Host applications do not validate the BLE peripheral.

Replay and forgery from recorded or public epochs, dataset level.
Temporal desynchronisation evasion.

items.rationale: Broadest 2026 empirical attack study found; preprint, so evidence weight is limited until peer review.
